articles.title: Katie Taylor vs Flora Pili: Bray native determined to sign off on her career in style
articles.summary: Katie Taylor is preparing for a stern test from Flora Pili rather than a Croke Park testimonial on Saturday night as she seeks to sign off on her career in style.
articles.body:
Katie Taylor is preparing for a stern test from Flora Pili rather than a Croke Park testimonial on Saturday night as she seeks to sign off on her career in style.

Over 54 years will have passed since Muhammad Ali headlined the last boxing event at the home of the Gaelic Athletic Association.

Just as 'The Greatest' blazed a trail in a career that transcended sport, Taylor has done likewise.

Elevating women's boxing to heights never experienced or perhaps expected, the 40-year-old will make her final walk in front of 80,000 fans with the opportunity to become undisputed champion at light-welterweight once again.

It is all set up for the glorious farewell, and while talk about ring-walks and musical entertainment is a feature of fight week in Dublin, Taylor is looking no further than her 29-year-old French opponent, who is perfect through 12 fights and holds the European and IBO belt.

"I'm trying not to think about it as I have a job to do," Taylor, whose record stands at 25-1, said at Tuesday's news conference when the subject of the overall event was raised.

"It's too dangerous a sport to have your body in the ring and your heart out of it, thinking of retirement.

"I have a job to do, and I'm very much focused on that job. The most important part of Saturday night is I get my hand raised, so it's business as usual for me.

"I've a live opponent in front of me, so it won't be a walk in the park. She is here to win ... a young, undefeated fighter. It will be a tough fight, but that's when I'm at my best."

There is truth to that final statement as her best performances have come when the danger was at its greatest: in the victories over Amanda Serrano, the rematch against Chantelle Cameron and in a 2020 rematch against Delfine Persoon which came 14 months after a much tighter battle in New York.

Pili, perhaps not keen on brash statements, has arrived in Ireland with braided hair in the colours of the French flag, and while few outside of her camp are predicting the upset, there is a quiet confidence.

"We're all aware of the task ahead but have the whole of France behind us, so we will be proud to take on Katie," said Pili, who is aware there is everything to gain should she spoil the party.

"I've nothing to lose and everything to win. I'm the underdog, and there is no pressure on me, so I will give everything I can from the first bell and take home all of these belts."

'Taylor has to focus on the fight' - Hearn

Taylor's sole career defeat came at the hands of Cameron in Dublin back in 2023 - a loss she later avenged to become undisputed champion in a second division - so there is certainly a realisation this is not a foregone conclusion on Saturday.

Undoubtedly, Cameron - whose only defeat came in that rematch against Taylor - has proven herself as a bona fide elite fighter, a status Pili is yet to reach.

While promoter Eddie Hearn is predicting "one of the greatest moments Irish sport has ever seen" on Saturday night, that will only fully come to pass should Taylor prevail.

"She's got to focus on the fight, because this girl's decent," said the Matchroom boss.

"I'm not saying she's got the pedigree of Katie Taylor, but Katie's 40 years old. She's [Taylor] fighting a young, strong girl who likes to trade, and so does Katie, who's IBO world champion, European champion, a decent amateur who can become undisputed herself on Saturday.

"She [Taylor] was saying, 'I need to prepare myself for war here', because she can't walk out, then get in the ring, and then it just passes you by, because that can happen.

"It will be an all-out war, because it's the only way she knows how to fight. She's not going to try to box and move because she'll want to leave it all in the ring."

Taylor is certainly making all the right noises in that regard and has been as methodical as ever in camp.

While she accepts it is "hard to prepare yourself for a moment I haven't experienced before" in terms of the overall occasion, she is determined to add one final glorious chapter to an already remarkable legacy.

"I'm not sure how I'm going to feel, but it will be a special night," she added.

"I'm going to walk to the ring, focus on the fight, as there will be plenty of time after to reflect on this amazing career, should I get my hand raised.

"I wouldn't be human if I didn't think of it all and think of all the little girls who may be at a boxing event for the first time.

"In my mind's eye, I think of one of those girls who might fall in love with this beautiful sport and may even surpass my achievements, all because of one amazing September day in Croke Park. I can't wait to hear those stories."

articles.title: Moses Itauma preparations questioned after defeat to Filip Hrgovic but heavyweight star is backed to become world champion
articles.summary: 'He didn't spar enough!' - Delicious Orie and Sam Noakes have queried if Moses Itauma did all he could in the build-up to his IBF world heavyweight title loss at the hands of unfancied Filip Hrgovic
articles.body:
Itauma was the overwhelming favourite heading into the bout but having dominated the opening eight rounds dramatically ran out of gas as he was stopped in the ninth.

Delicious Orie admits he was surprised by Itauma's pre-fight admission that he had not before sparred 12 rounds.

"It was experience. If I was getting a ring and knowing I've got 12 rounds ahead of me, I'm doing 15 rounds. For me, not doing 12 rounds going into a 12-round fight is crazy," he told Sky Sports.

"I guess it's each to their own. Moses boxed so perfectly but it was gradual rather than sudden. It goes back to experience. Hrgovic won that night because of it.

"He blew a gasket. This reminded me of new boxers in a new era taking strength and conditioning so seriously. You've got to find out about yourself before you get into the ring. You cannot learn on the job when it comes to professional boxing.

"I think he should have beaten Hrgovic. I wasn't in his training camps, but we've all heard it. He didn't spar enough; it's as simple as that. Just because you can lift weights or run fast does not mean you can sustain a 12-round fight. It's a completely different beast."

Like Itauma, lightweight contender Sam Noakes hails from Kent and has world title ambitions.

He agreed with Orie that inexperience contributed to Itauma's first career defeat, with the 21-year-old having to be taken to hospital following the fight.

"I think it was more Itauma beating himself. With all the success he was having, I think he might have just gone a little too fast out of the blocks. He wasn't out of his depth at all. It was more that he got tired and obviously Hrgovic capitalised on it," said Noakes.

"If he'd done a 12-rounder before maybe it might have helped. It's all well and good in hindsight but he was blasting out serious level opponents. That was the next step for him. He just came up short in a world title fight at 21. That's boxing unfortunately."

Itauma was bidding to become the second youngest man behind Mike Tyson to become world heavyweight champion.

However, having stopped all his opponents inside six rounds before facing Hrgovic, some have questioned whether the rising prospect was rushed into world title contention.

Orie disagrees with that notion and believes his promoter Frank Warren is the perfect man to help rebuild his career.

"I don't think he was being rushed. I think that was a good step up with Hrgovic. I do think there was a lot of hype. I don't think it would have had a massive impact on the fight. Itauma doesn't strike me as someone who loves all that hype. He's just a normal guy from Kent," he stated.

"Frank will more than anybody else know what the best thing is to do. I think his mindset is the question here. In his mind, his world's fallen apart. What he does in the next one or two years will be the deciding factor in my opinion for the rest of his boxing career."

Despite the setback, both Orie and Noakes are confident Itauma will recover and become world heavyweight champion in the future.

"One thing Itauma does have is the greatest asset known to man: time. 21 years old, he has a lot of time in front of him and depending on his mindset, this is just the beginning. This is part of becoming a world champion," Orie said.

"We've seen it time and time again with the likes of David Haye and [Wladimir] Klitschko losing in their early to mid-20s. It's the standard process.

"People just think it's smooth sailing, you turn professional, you beat Mike Tyson's record, you become world champion and retire into the sunset. Boxing doesn't work like that unfortunately and we've seen it here."

Meanwhile, Noakes added: "The experience everyone was saying he lacked, he has now gained. When he comes back, he'll be even better. As a fighter, the loss is terrible. It's like the end of the world.

"My advice to him would be just get back in the mix as quick as you can and back onto that world title chase. I have no doubt the ending will still be the same; he'll still be undisputed heavyweight champion."

articles.title: Kofi, Austin Creed reveal they were blindsided by WWE, asked to take 'more than 50%' pay cut
articles.summary: WWE legends Kofi Kingston and Xavier Woods — now Kofi and Austin Creed in AEW — clear the air on their messy WWE departure and how much of a pay cut they wer...
articles.body:
AEW All In 2026 delivered as one of the year's best professional wrestling events this past Sunday in London. On the grand stage of the world-famous Wembley Stadium, one of the annual spectacle's biggest moments was the debut of Kofi and Austin Creed — now known as The New Level after spending years in WWE as Kofi Kingston and Xavier Woods of The New Day.

The legendary duo wasn't advertised for the pay-per-view event, but instead made their arrival as a surprise entrant in the promotion's first-ever Trios Roulette Royale match for the AEW Trios Championships. Alongside Swerve Strickland, Kofi and Creed pulled off the win to become the new champions on only their first night on the job.

Kofi and Creed parted ways with WWE in a shocking development in May after a 12-year run teaming together, in addition to teaming with Big E. While Big E remained with the company as a retired wrestler-turned-analyst, Kofi and Creed were asked to take significant pay cuts when it came time to negotiate their contracts.

Speaking on Monday's edition of "The Ariel Helwani Show," they revealed that they only officially signed with AEW a day before All In. Regarding their WWE departure, the reported 50% pay-cut ask was incorrect: it was higher, according to Kofi.

"We just thought the terms that they wanted us to perform under were not fair based on what we brought to the table, based on what we're worth, based on the knowledge and prowess we have as performers and wrestlers," Kofi told Uncrowned. "What we can give back to the younger people and do in entertainment. Being able to go out there and garner a reaction as good guys or bad guys, no matter the situation. We took a lot of great pride in being Swiss Army knives. Whatever the situation was, we would make it great and make it entertaining. Compensation was definitely a big part, for sure, but more so, we wanted to work.

"I will say, it was more than 50%. It was more. The compensation is a big part of it, for sure, but the bigger part is being able to go out and live your dream in a way you want to live it out and be appreciated for it. We took it all into consideration, and we knew this was the only path to take."

Creed chimed in afterward when asked if there were any farewell messages from his longtime wrestling home. "Nope," he said when asked whether he received any thank-yous or calls upon leaving the company.

The process of adjusting to post-WWE life hit The New Level immediately, and even now, Kofi still struggles to call his longtime best friend "Creed" rather than "Woods" after having to leave the "Xavier Woods" name behind in WWE.

There was plenty of uncertainty in the early stages of their unemployment, said Kofi, who hadn't been a free agent in 20 years.

"This is so arrogant to say, but I'm just going to say it. I don't mean it in, like, a cocky way, but when you have the caliber of the career that we've had collectively as a group, you feel like you would not have to be in a position where you'd have to like, go in bet on yourselves again. But here we were," Kofi said.

"We found ourselves in that exact position, and as a father, if we didn't try to do this, if we didn't follow our hearts, how can I go back and tell my kids to go follow their dreams? To believe in themselves. To block out what people are saying about you and how they feel about you, and believe in yourself.

"If we didn't do that, I would feel like such a hypocrite, and I know Woods — Creed — feels the same way. That's going to take awhile; this time I caught myself. I had to change his name in my phone and everything. Like, bro, it's been a process. It's really trying to recalculate and recalibrate, but that's also a beautiful part of the whole process is being able to be reborn in a way. From a career standpoint, from a standpoint of having fun, from the standpoint of the uncertainty."

Ultimately, AEW was always the perfect landing spot for the all-time great tag team, said Creed. They never spoke to any other company before signing, largely because of the great tag scene AEW has cultivated throughout its existence.

In WWE, the tag-team division typically goes through waves of value for the company, and at its highest point in the past 15 years, Kofi and Creed were at the forefront. Injuries to their trio and the divisional fluctuation changed that, as they — and every other team — fell down the totem pole in recent years.

At AEW All In, specifically, the tag division was put on full display with a single image, coming directly after the current champions and all-time greats, Christian Cage and Adam Copeland, successfully defended against The Young Bucks.

"When it came to tag-team wrestling, it really wasn't a priority [in WWE], so we looked across the pond and saw the Bucks, FTR, Cope and Christian, Private Party, The Dogs, all these tag-teams having bangers," Kofi said. "'Man, what if we could be involved with that?' They look like they're having so much fun. You watch AEW pay-per-views, and I'm jumping out of my seat like a fan again. It excites me to watch that show.

"We're thinking, 'What if we could be part of that and add ourselves as one of, if not the greatest tag-team in history?' That was really the determining factor. Let's go and try to do what we love to do and feel passionate about our craft and feel like we're able to give in a way that is significant and matters. To go have bangers every night. That's what this is supposed to be. You're not supposed to go to work and feel frustrated with whatever is going on. You want to be able to have time to have matches that are incredible and entertaining. That's what the goal was."

Creed added to Kofi's sentiment as he examined the landscape in AEW. Despite holding WWE tag-team gold 12 times, there is still plenty more he sees for their future.

With all the fresh options at their disposal, it really is a tag-team playground of riches.

"We have a lot of friends over there, a lot of good people who said a lot of good things about it. But again, I know we probably sound like broken records to go back to the idea of having such a robust tag division and that being what our real focus is in this," Creed said.

"It just made a lot of sense to us, because watching those matches, watching those stories they get to tell — nobody is really doing it like that for tag-team wrestling. So it really just makes a lot of sense for us in that respect.

"I genuinely believe that this is the best tag-team division possibly ever. Like that shot at All In of all the tag-teams in the ring, that's some of the greatest tag-teams, I think, of our generation, so, possibly, when we're all done, maybe of all time, you know? And when are we going to get a chance to do something like that again? When has anyone ever done that in actuality? So, it really feels like, for the next duration, tag-team wrestling is going to be — they're eating well if they love tag wrestling."
